assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Uniform velocity
items.clue: Motion at the same speed in the same direction.

items.label: Newton's Third Law
items.clue: When two objects interact, the forces they exert on each other are equal and opposite.

items.label: Newton's Second Law
items.clue: Acceleration is proportional to the resultant force and inversely proportional to mass.

items.label: Newton's First Law
items.clue: With zero resultant force, a stationary object stays still and a moving one keeps the same velocity.

questions.stem: A crate rests on a level floor. Its weight is 400 N downwards and the floor pushes upwards on it with a force of 400 N. Which statement about the crate is correct?

options.text: The resultant force on the crate is zero, so it stays stationary.
No force at all acts on the crate while it is not moving.
The crate's weight and the floor's push are a third law pair.
The two forces add up to 800 N pressing on the floor.

questions.explanation: The two forces are equal in size and opposite in direction, so the resultant force is zero, and a stationary object with zero resultant force remains stationary.

questions.stem: The resultant force acting on a trolley is doubled while its mass is unchanged. What happens to the acceleration of the trolley?

options.text: Its speed doubles, but the acceleration stays as it was.
It halves, because the force has more work to do now.
It doubles, as acceleration is proportional to the resultant force.
It is unchanged, since the trolley's mass is the same.

questions.explanation: Newton's Second Law: the acceleration of an object is proportional to the resultant force acting on the object, so twice the force gives twice the acceleration.

questions.stem: A swimmer pushes backwards on the water with a force of 200 N. What force does the water exert on the swimmer?

options.text: Less than 200 N, because water is pushed aside so easily.
400 N forwards, twice as large as the swimmer's push.
200 N forwards, equal in size and opposite to her push.
200 N backwards, in the same direction as her push.

questions.explanation: Whenever two objects interact, the forces they exert on each other are equal and opposite, so the water pushes forwards on the swimmer with 200 N.

questions.stem: A puck slides in a straight line across a level ice rink at a steady 4 m/s. Friction and air resistance are so small that they can be ignored. What is the resultant force on the puck?

options.text: It acts forwards, because the puck is still moving forwards.
It is zero, because the puck's velocity is not changing.
It acts backwards, so the puck is very slowly stopping.
It is 4 N forwards, matching the puck's steady speed.

questions.explanation: The speed and the direction are both constant, so the velocity is constant, and by Newton's First Law the resultant force must be zero.

questions.stem: The mass of a trolley is trebled while the resultant force acting on it is kept the same. What happens to its acceleration?

options.text: It trebles, because the trolley is three times heavier.
It stays the same, since the force is unchanged.
It falls to a ninth of the value it had before.
The acceleration falls to a third of its old value.

questions.explanation: Acceleration is inversely proportional to the mass of the object, so three times the mass under the same resultant force gives one third of the acceleration.

questions.stem: A book rests in equilibrium on a table. Which two forces form a Newton's Third Law pair?

options.text: The weight of the book and the upward push of the table on the book.
The weight of the book and the friction between it and the table.
The table's push up and the floor's push up on the table.
The book's push down on the table and the table's push up on it.

questions.explanation: A third law pair is the two forces two interacting objects exert on each other: here the book on the table and the table on the book, equal and opposite.

questions.stem: A van travels along a straight level road at a steady 25 m/s. The driving force from its engine is 900 N. What can be said about the resistive forces on the van?

options.text: They are smaller than 900 N, which is why the van moves.
They are larger than 900 N, so the van is losing speed.
They total 900 N, acting backwards along the road.
They are zero, as the road surface is smooth.

questions.explanation: At a steady speed the resistive forces balance the driving force, so together they come to 900 N in the opposite direction.

questions.stem: A car of mass 1200 kg has a resultant force acting on it that gives it an acceleration of 2.5 m/s^2. What is the size of that resultant force?
questions.explanation: resultant force = mass x acceleration, so F = 1200 kg x 2.5 m/s^2 = 3000 N.

questions.stem: A horse pulls a cart forwards. The cart pulls back on the horse with an equal force. Why does the cart still accelerate?

options.text: The two forces act on different objects.
Because the horse is far stronger than the cart is.
It does not, so the loaded cart can never move.
The horse's pull comes a moment before the cart's.

questions.explanation: A third law pair never cancels, because only forces acting on the same object can be added; the cart accelerates because of the forces acting on the cart alone.

questions.stem: A car is driven all the way round a roundabout at a constant speed of 10 m/s. Is there a resultant force acting on the car?

options.text: No, since the speed stays at a steady 10 m/s.
No, the forces on the car must all be balanced.
Only if the driver presses the brake pedal.
Yes, because its direction is changing.

questions.explanation: Velocity is speed and direction. The direction changes continuously, so the velocity changes, and velocity only changes if a resultant force acts.

questions.stem: A go-kart and driver of total mass 500 kg have a driving force of 2500 N acting forwards on them and resistive forces of 500 N acting backwards. What is the acceleration?
questions.explanation: The resultant force is 2500 N - 500 N = 2000 N, so a = F / m = 2000 N / 500 kg = 4 m/s^2.

questions.stem: A skydiver falls at a constant terminal velocity before opening her parachute. Which statement explains her motion?

options.text: Her weight has fallen to zero, so nothing is pulling her downwards.
Her weight and the air resistance are equal, so the resultant is zero.
The air resistance is now larger than her weight as she falls.
A downward resultant force keeps her moving downwards at speed.

questions.explanation: A constant velocity means a zero resultant force, which here means the upward air resistance has grown until it balances her downward weight exactly.

questions.stem: (Higher tier) What is meant by the inertia of an object?

options.text: A forward force that keeps a moving object going.
A property that increases as an object moves faster.
The resistance of the air to an object moving through it.
Its tendency to stay at rest or in uniform motion.

questions.explanation: Inertia is exactly the tendency of objects to continue in their state of rest or of uniform motion.

questions.stem: (Higher tier) What does the inertial mass of an object measure?

options.text: The size of the gravitational pull acting on the object.
How difficult it is to change the object's velocity.
How fast the object is able to travel once it is released.
The force needed to keep the object still on Earth.

questions.explanation: Inertial mass is a measure of how difficult it is to change the velocity of an object.

questions.stem: (Higher tier) A bus brakes sharply and the standing passengers lurch forwards. Why does this happen?

options.text: They keep moving at their original velocity.
A forward force throws them out of their places.
Their inertia acts as a forward push on their bodies.
The braking force acts on the bus and then on them.

questions.explanation: Inertia: with no resultant backward force on them, the passengers continue in their state of uniform motion while the bus slows beneath them.

questions.stem: (Higher tier) How is inertial mass defined?

options.text: As the acceleration divided by the force.
As the weight of the object divided by 10 N/kg.
As the ratio of force over acceleration.
As the force multiplied by the acceleration.

questions.explanation: The specification defines inertial mass as the ratio of force over acceleration, matching m = F / a from F = m a.
